newsitem.title: USA: Study finds people often in severe pain while dying.
newsitem.headline: Study finds people often in severe pain while dying.

text.p: Severe pain and distress often mar the last days of life in modern society, according to a U.S. study published on Tuesday which could add new fuel to the debate on the "right to die" and doctor-assisted suicide.

The study, published in the current issue of Annals of Internal Medicine, reported that 40 percent of more than 3,000 seriously ill or elderly people it monitored experienced severe pain in the last three days of their lives.

Difficulties coping with emotional and physical problems commonly accompanied patients in their last days, and less than half the patients died without some last-ditch attempt to keep them alive, the report said.
"This study confirms widely held public fears that death is often difficult and undignified," said the study's lead author, Dr. Joanne Lynn of the George Washington University Medical Center.
"It is clear that we could do much, much better at alleviating pain, reducing isolation, and following patient wishes at the end of life," she said.
The study highligted dramatic changes since the last such study 90 years ago at Johns Hopkins Hospital found that death was a mostly quick and peaceful process.
"(For) the great majority...like their birth, their death was a sleep and a forgetting," the earlier study said.
Now, the new study said, "dying has become a gradual period of deterioration, and the once-familiar boundaries between 'being sick' and 'dying' have blurred."

Researchers in the new study followed 9,105 seriously ill patients and 1,176 people over 80, between 1989 and 1994. Of 4,622 subjects who died over the period, researchers interviewed family members of 3,357.
It said most of the patients, 59 percent, wanted treatment to focus on comforting them, even if it shortened their life.

Nearly three-fourths of the patients had difficulty coping with physical ailments such as shortness of breath, fatigue or nausea, and almost two-thirds -- 62 percent -- had emotional difficulties such as axiety or sadness.

But nearly one in 10 patients received care contrary to their wishes. Less than half -- 44 percent -- of all the patients died without being placed on a ventilator or feeding tube or undergoing a resuscitation attempt, it said.
It said changes would not occur in the treatment of dying people until the quality of care was routinely measured and the public and those who pay for health care demanded changes.

Last week, as the U.S. Supreme Court was taking up the issue of doctor-assisted suicide, Lynn told a news conference such suicides would be less of an issue if American society took better care of its dying.

An editorial with the study said the "right to die" movement was in part fueled by a fear that medical technololgy could cause people to lose control over their lives and cause them to experience a "lonely and impersonal death."

"Our society has not yet accepted the inevitability of death," it said. "We must change our attitudes and accept death as a natural phenomenon...We must provide our patients with a peaceful and dignified death, without pain and with as little anguish and anxiety as possible."
